author: PedroRaposo
body: Hello Pascale. Could we ask you for clarification of what the problem is, and how would you suggest to address it?

author: pgaudet
body:
Hi @PedroRaposo 

Sorry for the very short description of the problem. The conditions for that match is belonging to 
https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/entry/InterPro/IPR002223/ or https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/entry/InterPro/IPR036880/

These are described as trypsin inhibitors, not as potassium channels regulators. 
It seems to have some role in suppressing fibrinolysis  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23308198/ ? 
I dont know how widely accepted that it. If this is right, a better GO term would be 
[envenomation suppressing fibrinolysis in another organism](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/GO_0140099)
(just created yesterday!) 

cc-ing @FJungo in case she knows about this protein family. 

Thanks, Pascale

author: FJungo
body:
Hi Pedro and Pascale

in fact, there are many venom Kunitz-type proteins that have dual function, ie inhibiting potassium channels and inhibiting serine proteases.

https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb?query=%28xref%3Ainterpro-IPR002223%29+AND+%28keyword%3AKW-1220%29+AND+%28reviewed%3Atrue%29

I am currently updating this family. I tell you more in a few days.

author: FJungo
body:
Hello,

Of the 73 UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries corresponding to the ARBA request "ipr002223 AND ipr036880 AND chelicerata"
only 3 are described with plasmin inhibition activity. This activity has therefore been little studied in chelicerata. It is noteworthy that sometimes, such protease inhibitors have activity on one serine protease but not on another (eg. Trypsin vs. chymotrypsin). As a result, I personally wouldn't link 'GO:0140099; envenomation suppressing fibrinolysis in another organism' to the above-mentioned ARBA query.

In addition, potassium channel activity is low enough in the majority of cases to be ignored. I'll go ahead and modify the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries and strongly suggest deleting the association of 'GO:0044562; envenomation resulting in negative regulation of voltage-gated potassium channel activity in another organism' with the above-mentioned ARBA query.

A very nice day to both of you,
Florence

author: Antonialock
body:
this ARBA is now only applied to scorpions + ticks (one funfam has taxon restriction eukaryota but it is only found in scorpions and ticks). [It is applied to 39 proteins](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb?query=%28%28xref%3Ainterpro-IPR002223%29+AND+%28xref%3Ainterpro-IPR036880%29+AND+%28taxonomy_id%3A6855%29%29+OR+%28%28xref%3A%22funfam-4.10.410.10%3AFF%3A000072%22%29+AND+%28taxonomy_id%3A2759%29%29+OR+%28%28xref%3A%22funfam-3.30.30.10%3AFF%3A000009%22%29+AND+%28taxonomy_id%3A6886%29%29)

I found a [report ](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848636/) discussing the dual protease + K channel inhibitor functions:

"The dual effect toward protease and the ion channel detected here for ShPI-1 and reported in another five proteins from sea anemones ([Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848636/#toxins-08-00110-t003)) has been assumed as an economic manner to save energy and an advantage for these organisms from both an offensive and defensive point of view"

"According to [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848636/#B14-toxins-08-00110)], these molecules are survivors of a remote past in which evolution gave rise to more than one function in the same scaffold. Thus, the number of proteins acting on ion channels is rationalized, and the efficiency is increased, since the same polypeptide ensures: (i) the paralysis of the prey, though a toxic activity; and (ii) the protection against degradation of peptidic toxins injected into the prey, through the inhibition activity against proteases. Since ShPI-1 is able to inhibit a broad spectrum of serine proteases, including plasmin and kallikrein, it could ensure not only the protection of S. helianthus toxins, but also an additional effect on the prey’s enzymes."
